The enacted Electoral Count Act amendments clarified that the vice president’s role is ministerial and raised the threshold for congressional objections, while Congress—not the president alone—shaped the final law (E005). Executive Order 14074 established federal policing-accountability, misconduct-data, investigation, profiling, and reporting measures, although its reach over state and local policing was limited (E007). Federal protest-response guidance and a DOJ investigation into the NYPD’s Special Victims Division further show formal accountability activity, not completed nationwide outcomes (E030, E044). Press relations were more conventional than under the prior administration, but some press-freedom commitments remained incomplete (E045). Gubernatorial elections were described as largely peaceful with accredited observers, although vote-buying allegations implicated Tshisekedi’s coalition and remain unadjudicated (E008). Against this, Amnesty documented arbitrary detention, military trials of civilians, and killings connected to state-of-siege enforcement, while a UN report recorded a 49% rise in violations linked to restrictions on democratic space (E003, E036). Journalists and defenders faced arrest or threats, and peaceful assembly was restricted with deadly-force incidents reported (E006, E007). Civil-society criticism of CENI restructuring, calendar delays, and low institutional trust further weakened confidence in electoral independence, though these are not proof of a personal manipulation order (E009, E039, E051).
